author: reek
body: A definition beats a builtin. `emit-compound` has always implemented that -- it checks `user-arity < 0` before routing a call to `emit-builtin` -- but the constant folder decided the same question separately and decided it the other way, so a shadowed name answered TWO ways in one function depending on the shape of its argument.

author: reek
body: `text-length "abc"` has a literal argument, so `fold-apply` rewrote it to `3` at lowering time using the compiler's own `text-length`, and the definition below never ran. `text-length (substring "abcde" 0 3)` has a computed argument, no fold applies, and the definition answered 99. Same name, same body, same function, two answers.

author: reek
body: It was first recorded as per-BUILTIN -- `text-length` shadowed and `abs` did not -- which is why it read as a property of how each builtin lowers. It is per-CALL-SITE. `abs` looked well-behaved only because nothing folds `abs`; give `text-length` a non-literal argument and it was well-behaved too.

author: reek
body: So the test needs BOTH call sites and it needs them in one program. Either one alone passes against the broken compiler: the computed argument was always right, and the literal one is right the moment the fold declines. Only the pair shows that the two paths agree, which is the actual claim.

author: reek
body: `abs` is here as the control. It was never folded and never wrong, so if it ever changes, the fix went too far and started displacing builtins that nobody shadowed.
